entries.37734f3840608dd0936d79848971f67ebc82d6ca: <div sID="gen10763" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="24" osisID="Ps.24" sID="Ps.24"/> <div eID="gen10763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10764" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10765" type="x-p"/> This psalm is concerning the kingdom of Jesus Christ, I. His providential kingdom, by which he rules the world, <reference osisRef="Ps.24.1-Ps.24.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. II. The kingdom of his grace, by which he rules in his church. 1. Concerning the subjects of that kingdom; their character (<reference osisRef="Ps.24.4">ver. 4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.24.6">6</reference>), their charter, <reference osisRef="Ps.24.5">ver. 5</reference>. 2. Concerning the King of that kingdom; and a summons to all to give him admission, <reference osisRef="Ps.24.7-Ps.24.10">ver. 7-10</reference>. It is supposed that the psalm was penned upon occasion of David's bringing up the ark to the place prepared for it, and that the intention of it was to lead the people above the pomp of external ceremonies to a holy life and faith in Christ, of whom the ark was a type.
entries.726d196959ee51da3b6820d85ae84d3bf6609e7f: <div eID="gen10765" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10764" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">God's Absolute Propriety.</title> <div sID="gen10766" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The earth <hi type="italic">is</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's, and the fulness thereof; the world, and they that dwell therein. <hi type="super">2</hi> For he hath founded it upon the seas, and established it upon the floods. <div eID="gen10766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10767" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. God's absolute propriety in this part of the creation where our lot is cast, <reference osisRef="Ps.24.1">v. 1</reference>. We are not to think that the heavens, even the heavens only, are the Lord's, and the numerous and bright inhabitants of the upper world, and that this earth, being so small and inconsiderable a part of the creation, and at such a distance from the royal palace above, is neglected, and that he claims no interest in it. No, even the earth is his, and this lower world; and, though he has prepared the throne of his glory in the heavens, yet his kingdom rules over all, and even the worms of this earth are not below his cognizance, nor from under his dominion. 1. When God gave the earth to the children of men he still reserved to himself the property, and only let it out to them as tenants, or usufructuaries: <hi type="italic">The earth is the Lord's and the fulness thereof.</hi> The mines that are lodged in the bowels of it, even the richest, the fruits it produces, all the beasts of the forest and the cattle upon a thousand hills, our lands and houses, and all the improvements that are made of this earth by the skill and industry of man, are all his. These indeed, in the kingdom of grace, are justly looked upon as emptiness; for they are vanity of vanities, nothing to a soul; but, in the kingdom of providence, they are fulness. <hi type="italic">The earth is full of God's riches, so is the great and wide sea also.</hi> All the parts and regions of the earth are the Lord's, all under his eye, all in his hand: so that, wherever a child of God goes, he may comfort himself with this, that he does not go off his Father's ground. That which falls to our share of the earth and its productions is but lent to us; it is the Lord's; what is our own against all the world is not so against his claims. That which is most remote from us, as that which passes through the paths of the sea, or is hidden in the bottom of it, is the Lord's and he knows where to find it. 2. The habitable part of this earth (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.31">Prov. viii. 31</reference>) is his in a special manner—<hi type="italic">the world and those that dwell therein.</hi> We ourselves are not our own, our bodies, our souls, are not. <hi type="italic">All souls are mine,</hi> says God; for he is the former of our bodies and the Father of our spirits. Our tongues are not our own; they are to be at his service. Even those of the children of men that know him not, nor own their relation to him, are his. Now this comes in here to show that, though God is graciously pleased to accept the devotions and services of his peculiar chosen people (<reference osisRef="Ps.24.3-Ps.24.5">v. 3-5</reference>), it is not because he needs them, or can be benefited by them, for the earth is his and all in it, <reference osisRef="Exod.19.5">Exod. xix. 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.50.12">Ps. l. 12</reference>. It is likewise to be applied to the dominion Christ has, as Mediator, over the utmost parts of the earth, which are given him for his possession: the Father loveth the Son and hath given all things into his hand, power over all flesh. The apostle quotes this scripture twice together in his discourse about things offered to idols, <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.26">1 Cor. x. 26</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.28">28</reference>. "If it be sold in the shambles, eat it, and ask no questions; <hi type="italic">for the earth is the Lord's;</hi> it is God's good creature, and you have a right to it. But, if one tell you it was offered to an idol, forbear, <hi type="italic">for the earth is the Lord's,</hi> and there is enough besides." This is a good reason why we should be content with our allotment in this world, and not envy others theirs; <hi type="italic">the earth is the Lord's,</hi> and may he not do what he will with his own, and give to some more of it, to others less, as it pleases him? <div eID="gen10767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10768" type="x-p"/> II. The ground of this propriety. The earth is his by an indisputable title, <hi type="italic">for he hath founded it upon the seas</hi> and <hi type="italic">established it upon the floods,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.24.2">v. 2</reference>. It is his; for, 1. He made it, formed it, founded it, and fitted it for the use of man. The matter is his, for he made it out of nothing; the form is his, for he made it according to the eternal counsels and ideas of his own mind. He made it himself, he made it for himself; so that he is sole, entire, and absolute owner, and none can let us a title to any part, but by, from, and under him; see <reference osisRef="Ps.89.11-Ps.89.12">Ps. lxxxix. 11, 12</reference>. 2. He made it so as no one else could. It is the creature of omnipotence, for it is founded upon the seas, upon the floods, a weak and unstable foundation (one would think) to build the earth upon, and yet, if almighty power please, it shall serve to bear the weight of this earth. The waters which at first covered the earth, and rendered it unfit to be a habitation for man, were ordered under it, that the dry land might appear, and so they are as a foundation to it; see <reference osisRef="Ps.104.8-Ps.104.9">Ps. civ. 8, 9</reference>. 3. He continues it, he has <hi type="italic">established</hi> it, fixed it, so that, though one generation passes and another comes, the earth abides, <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.4">Eccl. i. 4</reference>. And his providence is a continued creation, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.90">Ps. cxix. 90</reference>. The founding of the earth upon the floods should remind us how slippery and uncertain all earthly things are; their foundation is not only sand, but water; it is therefore our folly to build upon them.
entries.1355891d4a332bb5fd5dd6029ef94ce808d34ace: <div eID="gen10768" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Character of True Israelites.</title> <div sID="gen10769" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">3</hi> Who shall ascend into the hill of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ? or who shall stand in his holy place? <hi type="super">4</hi> He that hath clean hands, and a pure heart; who hath not lifted up his soul unto vanity, nor sworn deceitfully. 5 He shall receive the blessing from the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and righteousness from the God of his salvation. <hi type="super">6</hi> This <hi type="italic">is</hi> the generation of them that seek him, that seek thy face, O Jacob. Selah. <div eID="gen10769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10770" type="x-p"/> From this world, and the fulness thereof, the psalmist's meditations rise, of a sudden to the great things of another world, the foundation of which is not on the seas, nor on the floods. The things of this world God has given to the children of men and we are much indebted to his providence for them; but they will not make a portion for us. And therefore, <div eID="gen10770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10771" type="x-p"/> I. Here is an enquiry after better things, <reference osisRef="Ps.24.3">v. 3</reference>. This earth is God's footstool; but, if we had ever so much of it, we must be here but a while, must shortly go hence, and <hi type="italic">Who then shall ascend into the hill of the Lord?</hi> Who shall go to heaven hereafter, and, as an earnest of that, shall have communion with God in holy ordinances now? A soul that knows and considers its own nature, origin, and immortality, when it has viewed the earth and the fulness thereof, will sit down unsatisfied; there is not found among all the creatures a help meet for man, and therefore it will think of ascending towards God, towards heaven, will ask, "What shall I do to rise to that high place, that hill, where the Lord dwells and manifests himself, that I may be acquainted with him, and to abide in that happy holy place where he meets his people and makes them holy and happy? What shall I do that I may be of those whom God owns for his peculiar people and who are his in another manner than the earth is his and its fulness?" This question is much the same with that, <reference osisRef="Ps.15.1">Ps. xv. 1</reference>. The hill of Zion on which the temple was built typified the church, both visible and invisible. When the people attended the ark to its holy place David puts them in mind that these were but patterns of heavenly things, and therefore that by them they should be led to consider the heavenly things themselves. <div eID="gen10771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10772" type="x-p"/> II. An answer to this enquiry, in which we have, <div eID="gen10772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10773" type="x-p"/> 1. The properties of God's peculiar people, who shall have communion with him in grace and glory. (1.) They are such as keep themselves from all the gross acts of sin. They have <hi type="italic">clean hands;</hi> not spotted with the pollutions of the world and the flesh. None that were ceremonially unclean might enter into the mountain of the temple, which signified that cleanness of conversation which is required in all those that have fellowship with God. The hands lifted up in prayer must be pure hands, no blot of unjust gain cleaving to them, nor any thing else that defiles the man and is offensive to the holy God. (2.) They are such as make conscience of being really (that is, of being inwardly) as good as they seem to be outwardly. They have <hi type="italic">pure hearts.</hi> We make nothing of our religion if we do not make heart-work of it. It is not enough that our hands be clean before men, but we must also wash our hearts from wickedness, and not allow ourselves in any secret heart-impurities, which are open before the eye of God. Yet in vain do those pretend to have pure and good hearts whose hands are defiled with the acts of sin. That is a pure heart which is sincere and without guile in covenanting with God, which is carefully guarded, that the wicked one, the unclean spirit, touch it not, which is purified by faith, and conformed to the image and will of God; see <reference osisRef="Matt.5.8">Matt. v. 8</reference>. (3.) They are such as do not set their affections upon the things of this world, do not <hi type="italic">lift up their souls unto vanity,</hi> whose hearts are not carried out inordinately towards the wealth of this world, the praise of men, or the delights of sense, who do not choose these things for their portion, nor reach forth after them, because they believe them to be vanity, uncertain and unsatisfying. (4.) They are such as deal honestly both with God and man. In their covenant with God, and their contracts with men, they have not sworn deceitfully, nor broken their promises, violated their engagements, nor taken any false oath. Those that have no regard to the obligations of truth or the honour of God's name are unfit for a place in God's holy hill. (5.) They are a praying people (<reference osisRef="Ps.24.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">This is the generation of those that seek him.</hi> In every age there is a remnant of such as these, men of this character, who are <hi type="italic">accounted to the Lord for a generation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.22.30">Ps. xxii. 30</reference>. And they are such as seek God, <hi type="italic">that seek thy face, O Jacob!</hi> [1.] They join themselves to God, to seek him, not only in earnest prayer, but in serious endeavours to obtain his favour and keep themselves in his love. Having made it the summit of their happiness, they make it the summit of their ambition to be accepted of him, and therefore take care and pains to approve themselves to him. It is to the hill of the Lord that we must ascend, and, the way being up-hill, we have need to put forth ourselves to the utmost, as those that seek diligently. [2.] They join themselves to the people of God, to seek God with them. Being brought into communion with God, they come into communion of saints; conforming to the patterns of the saints that have gone before (so some understand this), they seek God's face, as Jacob (so some), who was <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> surnamed <hi type="italic">Israel,</hi> because he wrestled with God and prevailed, sought him and found him; and, associating with the saints of their own day, they shall court the favour of God's church (<reference osisRef="Rev.3.9">Rev. iii. 9</reference>), shall be glad of an acquaintance with God's people (<reference osisRef="Zech.8.23">Zech. viii. 23</reference>), shall incorporate themselves with them, and, when they <hi type="italic">subscribe with their hands to the Lord,</hi> shall <hi type="italic">call themselves by the name of Jacob,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.44.5">Isa. xliv. 5</reference>. As soon as ever Paul was converted he <hi type="italic">joined himself to the disciples,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.9.26">Acts ix. 26</reference>. They shall seek God's face <hi type="italic">in Jacob</hi> (so some), that is, in the assemblies of his people. <hi type="italic">Thy face, O God of Jacob!</hi> so our margin supplies it, and makes it easy. As all believers are the spiritual seed of Abraham, so all that strive in prayer are the spiritual seed of Jacob, to whom God never said, <hi type="italic">Seek you me in vain.</hi> <div eID="gen10773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10774" type="x-p"/> 2. The privileges of God's peculiar people, <reference osisRef="Ps.24.5">v. 5</reference>. They shall be made truly and for ever happy. (1.) They shall be blessed: they shall receive the blessing from the Lord, all the fruits and gifts of God's favour, according to his promise; and those whom God blesses are blessed indeed, for it is his prerogative to command the blessing. (2.) They shall be justified and sanctified. These are the spiritual blessings in heavenly things which they shall receive, even righteousness, the very thing they hunger and thirst after, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.5">Matt. v. 6</reference>. Righteousness is blessedness, and it is from God only that we must expect it, for we have no righteousness of our own. They shall receive the reward of their righteousness (so some), the <hi type="italic">crown of righteousness which the righteous Judge shall give,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.8">2 Tim. iv. 8</reference>. (3.) They shall be saved; for God himself will be the God of their salvation. Note, Where God gives righteousness he certainly designs salvation. Those that are made meet for heaven shall be brought safely to heaven, and then they will find what they have been seeking, to their endless satisfaction.
entries.d6925a9b5b4c9d2187f56dd80d50e8200805f0d3: <div eID="gen10774" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The King of Glory.</title> <div sID="gen10775" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> Lift up your heads, O ye gates; and be ye lift up, ye everlasting doors; and the King of glory shall come in. 8 Who <hi type="italic">is</hi> this King of glory? The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> strong and mighty, the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> mighty in battle. <hi type="super">9</hi> Lift up your heads, O ye gates; even lift <hi type="italic">them</hi> up, ye everlasting doors; and the King of glory shall come in. <hi type="super">10</hi> Who is this King of glory? The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, he <hi type="italic">is</hi> the King of glory. Selah. <div eID="gen10775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10776" type="x-p"/> What is spoken once is spoken a second time in these verses; such repetitions are usual in songs, and have much beauty in them. Here is, 1. Entrance once and again demanded for the King of glory; the doors and gates are to be thrown open, thrown wide open, to give him admission, for behold he stands at the door and knocks, ready to come in. 2. Enquiry once and again made concerning this mighty prince, in whose name entrance is demanded: <hi type="italic">Who is this King of glory?</hi> As, when any knock at our door, it is common to ask, <hi type="italic">Who is there?</hi> 3. Satisfaction once and again given concerning the royal person that makes the demand: <hi type="italic">It is the Lord, strong and mighty, the Lord, mighty in battle, the Lord of hosts,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.24.8">v. 8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.24.10">10</reference>. Now, <div eID="gen10776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10777" type="x-p"/> I. This splendid entry here described it is probable refers to the solemn bringing in of the ark into the tent David pitched for it or the temple Solomon built for it; for, when David prepared materials for the building of it, it was proper for him to prepare a psalm for the dedication of it. The porters are called upon to open the doors, and they are called <hi type="italic">everlasting doors,</hi> because much more durable than the door of the tabernacle, which was but a curtain. They are taught to ask, <hi type="italic">Who is this King of glory?</hi> And those that bore the ark are taught to answer in the language before us, and very fitly, because the ark was a symbol or token of God's presence, <reference osisRef="Josh.3.11">Josh. iii. 11</reference>. Or it may be taken as a poetical figure designed to represent the subject more affectingly. God, in his word and ordinances, is thus to be welcomed by us, 1. With great readiness: the doors and gates must be thrown open to him. Let the word of the Lord come into the innermost and uppermost place in our souls; and, if we had 600 necks, we should bow them all to the authority of it. 2. With all reverence, remembering how great a God he is with whom we have to do, in all our approaches to him. <div eID="gen10777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10778" type="x-p"/> II. Doubtless it points at Christ, of whom the ark, with the mercy-seat, was a type. 1. We may apply it to the ascension of Christ into heaven and the welcome given to him there. When he had finished his work on earth he ascended <hi type="italic">in the clouds of heaven,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.7.13-Dan.7.14">Dan. vii. 13, 14</reference>. The gates of heaven must then be opened to him, those doors that may be truly called <hi type="italic">everlasting,</hi> which had been shut against us, to keep the way of the tree of life, <reference osisRef="Gen.3.24">Gen. iii. 24</reference>. Our Redeemer found them shut, but, having by his blood made atonement for sin and gained a title to <hi type="italic">enter into the holy place</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.9.12">Heb. ix. 12</reference>), as one having authority, he demanded entrance, not for himself only, but for us; for, as the forerunner, he has for us entered and <hi type="italic">opened the kingdom of heaven to all believers.</hi> The keys not only of hell and death, but of heaven and life, must be put into his hand. His approach being very magnificent, the angels are brought in asking, <hi type="italic">Who is this King of glory?</hi> For angels keep the gates of the New Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Rev.21.12">Rev. xxi. 12</reference>. When the first-begotten was brought into the upper world the angels were to worship him (<reference osisRef="Heb.1.6">Heb. i. 6</reference>); and accordingly, they here ask with wonder, "Who is he?—this that cometh <hi type="italic">with dyed garments from Bozrah?</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.63.1-Isa.63.3">Isa. lxiii. 1-3</reference>), for he appears in that world <hi type="italic">as a Lamb that had been slain.</hi>" It is answered that he is <hi type="italic">strong and mighty, mighty in battle,</hi> to save his people and subdue his and their enemies. 2. We may apply it to Christ's entrance into the souls of men by his word and Spirit, that they may be his temples. Christ's presence in them is like that of the ark in the temple; it sanctifies them. <hi type="italic">Behold, he stands at the door and knocks,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.3.20">Rev. iii. 20</reference>. It is required that the gates and doors of the heart be opened to him, not only as admission is given to a guest, but as possession is delivered to the rightful owner, after the title has been contested. This is the gospel call and demand, that we let Jesus Christ, the King of glory, come into our souls, and welcome him with hosannas, <hi type="italic">Blessed is he that cometh.</hi> That we may do this aright we are concerned to ask, <hi type="italic">Who is this King of glory?</hi>—to acquaint ourselves with him, whom we are to believe in, and to love above all. And the answer is ready: He is <hi type="italic">Jehovah,</hi> and will be <hi type="italic">Jehovah our righteousness,</hi> an all-sufficient Saviour to us, if we give him entrance and entertainment. He is <hi type="italic">strong and mighty,</hi> and <hi type="italic">the Lord of hosts;</hi> and therefore it is at our peril if we deny him entrance; for he is able to avenge the affront; he can force his way, and can break those in pieces with his iron rod that will not submit to his golden sceptre. <div eID="gen10778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10779" type="x-p"/> In singing this let our hearts cheerfully answer to this call, as it is in the first words of the next psalm, <hi type="italic">Unto thee, O Lord! do I lift up my soul.</hi>  <chapter eID="Ps.24"/> <div eID="gen10779" type="x-p"/>

entries.cb6fc8f72d9618c6c8f2d42fb395ee846a67debf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5706"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 24</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.24.1-Ps.24.10">Psa 24:1-10</reference>. God's supreme sovereignty requires a befitting holiness of life and heart in His worshippers; a sentiment sublimely illustrated by describing His entrance into the sanctuary, by the symbol of His worship--the ark, as requiring the most profound homage to the glory of His Majesty.</title> <div sID="gen8686" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5706"/><hi type="bold">1. fulness--</hi>everything.<div eID="gen8686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8687" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">world--</hi>the habitable globe, with<div eID="gen8687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8688" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they that dwell--</hi>forming a parallel expression to the first clause. <div eID="gen8688" type="x-p"/>

entries.e904404f9e50ebda1ca2e484f396f2e898f85d1f: <div eID="gen19273" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen19274" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19275" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19275" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19274" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19276" type="x-p"/> The Lord is Sovereign Ruler of the universe, <reference osisRef="Psa.24.1">Psa 24:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.24.2">Psa 24:2</reference>. The great question, Who is fit to minister to the Lord in his own temple? <reference osisRef="Psa.24.3-Psa.24.6">Psa 24:3-6</reference>. The glory of God in his entrance into his temple, <reference osisRef="Psa.24.7-Psa.24.10">Psa 24:7-10</reference>. <div eID="gen19276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19277" type="x-p"/> It is probable that this Psalm was composed on occasion of bringing the ark from the house of Obed-edom to Mount Sion, and the questions may respect the fitness of the persons who were to minister before this ark: the last verses may refer to the opening of the city gates in order to admit it. As many of the expressions here are nearly the same with those in <reference osisRef="Psa.15.1-Psa.15.5">Psa 15:1-5</reference>, I must refer to that place for their particular illustration; though it is most likely that the two Psalms were composed on very different occasions. The first contains a general question relative to who shall be saved? This is more particular; and refers to the temple and tabernacle service, and who is fit to minister there. <div eID="gen19277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19278" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen19278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19279" type="x-p"/> The earth is the Lord's - He is the Creator and Governor of it; it is his own property. Men may claim districts and kingdoms of it as their property, but God is Lord of the soil. <div eID="gen19279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19280" type="x-p"/> The fullness thereof - "All its creatures." - Targum. Every tree, plant, and shrub; the silver and the gold, and the cattle on a thousand hills. <div eID="gen19280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19281" type="x-p"/> They that dwell therein - All human beings.
entries.0641ad7269a3dfba6812e8500cd4d2385e764b31: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen19281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19282" type="x-p"/> He hath founded it upon the seas - He not only created the vast mass, but separated the land from the waters, so that the mountains, etc., being elevated above the waters, appear to be founded on them, and notwithstanding all the tossings and ragings of the ocean, these waters cannot prevail. It is established upon the floods, and cannot be shaken.
entries.fbcbd60ef0fb91d49a28ada1762752bb358156ca: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen19282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19283" type="x-p"/> Who shall ascend - Who is sufficiently holy to wait in his temple? Who is fit to minister in the holy place?
entries.2317a9763c553b1ef7edd2fcd2713534f73d60b2: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen19283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19284" type="x-p"/> He that hath clean hands - He whose conscience is irreproachable; whose heart is without deceit and uninfluenced by unholy passions. <div eID="gen19284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19285" type="x-p"/> Who hath not lifted up his soul - Who has no idolatrous inclination; whose faith is pure, and who conscientiously fulfils his promises and engagements.
entries.be24c746408fe635beb99bf4a01060aa0c820699: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen19285" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19286" type="x-p"/> He shall receive the blessing - Perhaps alluding to Obed-edom, at whose house the ark had been lodged, and on whom God had poured out especial blessings. <div eID="gen19286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19287" type="x-p"/> And righteousness - Mercy: every kind of necessary good. It is the mercy of God that crowns the obedience and fidelity of good men. For what made them good and faithful? God's mercy. What crowns their fidelity? God's mercy.
entries.b50737d30cf4d9fe95421fd03c388bd9a263ef34: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen19287" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19288" type="x-p"/> This is the generation - This is the description of people who are such as God can approve of, and delight in. <div eID="gen19288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19289" type="x-p"/> That seek thy face, O Jacob - It is most certain that אלהי Elohey, O God, has been lost out of the Hebrew text in most MSS., but it is preserved in two of Kennicott's MSS., and also in the Syriac, Vulgate, Septuagint, Ethiopic, Arabic, and Anglo-Saxon. "Who seek thy face, O God of Jacob." <div eID="gen19289" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19290" type="x-p"/> Selah - That is, It is confirmed; it is true. The persons who abstain from every appearance of evil, and seek the approbation of God, are those in whom God will delight.
entries.ce1caa205b3f2f549b9b187001a753d9c0e08521: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen19290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19291" type="x-p"/> Lift up your heads, O ye gates - The address of those who preceded the ark, the gates being addressed instead of the keepers of the gates. Allusion is here made to the triumphal entry of a victorious general into the imperial city. <div eID="gen19291" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19292" type="x-p"/> In the hymn of Callimachus to Apollo, there are two lines very much like those in the text; they convey the very same sentiments. The poet represents the god coming into his temple, and calls upon the priests to open the doors, etc. Αυτοι νυν κατοχηες ανακλινεσθε πυλαως, Αυται δε κληιδες· ὁ γαρ Θεος ουκ ετι μακραν; "Fall back, ye bolts; ye pond'rous doors, give way <div eID="gen19292" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19293" type="x-p"/> For not far distant is the god of day." <div eID="gen19293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19294" type="x-p"/> Callim. Hymn in Apol., ver. 6, 7. <div eID="gen19294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19295" type="x-p"/> The whole of this hymn contains excellent sentiments even on the subject of the Psalms. <div eID="gen19295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19296" type="x-p"/> Everlasting doors - There seems to be a reference here to something like our portcullis, which hangs by pullies above the gate, and can be let down at any time so as to prevent the gate from being forced. In the case to which the psalmist refers, the portcullis is let down, and the persons preceding the ark order it to be raised. When it is lifted up, and appears above the head or top of the gate, then the folding doors are addressed: "Be ye lift up, ye everlasting doors;" let there be no obstruction; and the mighty Conqueror, the King of glory, whose presence is with the ark, and in which the symbol of his glory appears, shall enter. Make due preparations to admit so august and glorious a Personage.
entries.7d2ead09a6fb4c3c792301fcce9c38283723fbe5: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen19296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19297" type="x-p"/> Who is this King of glory? - This is the answer of those who are within. Who is this glorious King, for whom ye demand entrance? To which they reply: - <div eID="gen19297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19298" type="x-p"/> The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle - It is Jehovah, who is come to set up his abode in his imperial city: He who has conquered his enemies, and brought salvation to Israel. To make the matter still more solemn, and give those without an opportunity of describing more particularly this glorious Personage, those within hesitate to obey the first summons: and then it is repeated, <reference osisRef="Psa.24.9">Psa 24:9</reference>. <div eID="gen19298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19299" type="x-p"/> Lift up your heads, O ye gates; even lift them up, ye everlasting doors; and the King of glory shall come in - To which a more particular question is proposed: - Who is He, This King of glory? To which an answer is given that admitted of no reply. The Lord of hosts - he who is coming with innumernble armies, He is this King of glory. On which, we may suppose, the portcullis was lifted up, the gates thrown open, and the whole cavalcade admitted. This verse seems to have been spoken before the ark appeared: Who is this (זה zeh) King of glory? when its coming was merely announced. In the tenth verse the form is a little altered, because the ark, the symbol of the Divine Presence, had then arrived. Who is He, (מי הוא mi hu), this King of glory? Here He is, to answer for himself. "The Lord is in his holy temple; let all the earth keep silence before him." <div eID="gen19299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19300" type="x-p"/> Though this Psalm has all the appearance of being an unfinished piece, yet there is a vast deal of dignity and majesty in it; and the demands from without, the questions from those within, and the answers to those questions, partake of the true sublime; where nature, dignity, and simplicity, are very judiciously mingled together. The whole procedure is natural, the language dignified, and the questions and answers full of simplicity and elevated sentiments. <div eID="gen19300" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19301" type="x-p"/> Several, both among ancients and moderns, have thought this Psalm speaks of the resurrection of our Lord, and is thus to be understood. It is easy to apply it in this way: Jesus has conquered sin, Satan, and death, by dying. He now rises from the dead; and, as a mighty Conqueror, claims an entrance into the realms of glory, the kingdom which he has purchased by his blood; there to appear ever in the presence of God for us, to which he purposes to raise finally the innumerable hosts of his followers; for in reference to these, He is the Lord of hosts; and, in reference to his victory, He is the Lord mighty in battle.  <chapter eID="Ps.24"/> <div eID="gen19301" type="x-p"/>

entries.b189d47d9b0eb8f463075267b601ae3a4736f675: <div eID="gen9292" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Preparation for the Reception of the Lord Who Is About to Come</title> <div sID="gen9293" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Ps.23.1-Ps.23.6">Psa 23:1-6</reference> expressed a longing after the house of Jahve on Zion; <reference osisRef="Ps.24.1-Ps.24.10">Psa 24:1-10</reference> celebrates Jahve’s entrance into Zion, and the true character of him who may enter with Him. It was composed when the Ark was brought from Kirjath Jearim to Mount Zion, where David had caused it to be set up in a tabernacle built expressly for it, <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.17">2Sa 6:17</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="2Sam.11.11">2Sa 11:11</reference>, 1Ki 1:39; or else, which is rendered the more probable by the description of Jahve as a warrior, at a time when the Ark was brought back to Mount Zion, after having been taken to accompany the army to battle (vid., Ps 68). <reference osisRef="Ps.15.1-Ps.15.5">Psa 15:1-5</reference> is very similar. But only <reference osisRef="Ps.24.1-Ps.24.6">Psa 24:1-6</reference> is the counterpart of that Psalm; and there is nothing wanting to render the first part of <reference osisRef="Ps.24.1-Ps.24.10">Psa 24:1-10</reference> complete in itself. Hence Ewald divides <reference osisRef="Ps.24.1-Ps.24.10">Psa 24:1-10</reference> into two songs, belonging to different periods, although both old Davidic songs, viz., <reference osisRef="Ps.24.7-Ps.24.10">Psa 24:7-10</reference>, the song of victory sung at the removal of the Ark to Zion; and <reference osisRef="Ps.24.1-Ps.24.6">Psa 24:1-6</reference>, a purely didactic song pre-supposing this event which forms an era in their history. And it is relatively more natural to regard this Psalm rather than <reference osisRef="Ps.19.1-Ps.19.14">Psa 19:1-14</reference>, as two songs combined and made into one; but these two songs have an internal coherence; in Jahve’s coming to His temple is found that which occasioned them and that towards which They point; and consequently they form a whole consisting of two divisions. To the inscription לדוד מזמור the lxx adds τῆς μιᾷs σαββάτου<note placement="foot">The London Papyrus fragments, in Tischendorf <hi type="italic">Monum</hi>. i. 247, read ΤΗ ΜΙΑ ΤΩΝ ΣΑΒΒΑΤΩΝ. In the Hexaplarian text, this addition to the inscription was wanting.</note> (= שׁל אחד בשׁבת, for the first day of the week), according to which this Psalm was a customary Sunday Psalm. This addition is confirmed by <hi type="italic">B . Tamı̂d extr ., Rosh ha - Shana</hi> 31 <hi type="italic">a</hi>, <hi type="italic">Sofrim</hi> xviii. (cf. <hi type="italic">supra</hi> p. 19). In the second of these passages cited from the Talmud, R. Akiba seeks to determine the reasons for this choice by reference to the history of the creation. <div eID="gen9293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9294" type="x-p"/> Incorporated in Israel’s hymn-book, this Psalm became, with a regard to its original occasion and purpose, an Old Testament Advent hymn in honour of the Lord who should come into His temple, Mal 3:1; and the cry: Lift up, ye gates, your heads, obtained a meaning essentially the same as that of the voice of the crier in <reference osisRef="Isa.40.3">Isa 40:3</reference> : Prepare ye Jahve’s way, make smooth in the desert a road for our God! In the New Testament consciousness, the second appearing takes the place of the first, the coming of the Lord of Glory to His church, which is His spiritual temple; and in this Psalm we are called upon to prepare Him a worthy reception. The interpretation of the second half of the Psalm of the entry of the Conqueror of death into Hades-an interpretation which has been started by the Gospel of Nicodemus (vid., Tischendorf’s <hi type="italic">Evv. apocrypha</hi> p. 306f.) and still current in the Greek church, - and the patristic interpretation of it of the εἰς οὐρανοῦς ἀνάληψις τοῦ κυρίου, do as much violence to the rules of exegesis as to the parallelism of the facts of the Old and New Testaments.
entries.89c474a6adfedbd0296541e25c17c23b801e4682: <reference osisRef="Ps.24.1-Ps.24.6">Psa 24:1-6</reference> <div eID="gen9294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9295" type="x-p"/> Jahve, whose throne of grace is now set upon Zion, has not a limited dominion, like the heathen deities: His right to sovereignty embraces the earth and its fulness (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.12">Psa 50:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.89.12">Psa 89:12</reference>), i.e., everything that is to be found upon it and in it.<note placement="foot">In <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.26">1Co 10:26</reference>, Paul founds on this verse (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.50.12">Psa 50:12</reference>) the doctrine that a Christian (apart from a charitable regard for the weak) may eat whatever is sold in the shambles, without troubling himself to enquire whether it has been offered to idols or not. A Talmudic teacher, <hi type="italic">B. Berachoth 35a</hi>, infers from this passage the duty of prayer before meat: He who eats without giving thanks is like one who lays hands upon קדשׁי שׁמים (the sacred things of God); the right to eat is only obtained by prayer.</note> <div eID="gen9295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9296" type="x-p"/> For He, הוא, is the owner of the world, because its Creator. He has founded it upon seas, i.e., the ocean and its streams, נהרות, ῥέεθρα (<reference osisRef="Jonah.2.4">Jon 2:4</reference>); for the waters existed before the dry land, and this has been cast up out of them at God’s word, so that consequently the solid land, - which indeed also conceals in its interior a תּהום רבּה (<reference osisRef="Gen.7.11">Gen 7:11</reference>), - rising above the surface of the sea, has the waters, as it were, for its foundation (<reference osisRef="Ps.136.6">Psa 136:6</reference>), although it would more readily sink down into them than keep itself above them, if it were not in itself upheld by the creative power of God. Hereupon arises the question, who may ascend the mountain of Jahve, and stand above in His holy place? The futures have a potential signification: who can have courage to do it? what, therefore, must he be, whom Jahve receives into His fellowship, and with whose worship He is well-pleased? Answer: he must be one innocent in his actions and pure in mind, one who does not lift up his soul to that which is vain (לשּׁוא, according to the Masora with <hi type="italic">Waw minusculum</hi>). (ל) נשׂא נפשׁ אל, to direct one’s soul, <reference osisRef="Ps.25.1">Psa 25:1</reference>, or longing and striving, towards anything, <reference osisRef="Deut.24.15">Deu 24:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.19.18">Pro 19:18</reference>; Hos 4:8. The <hi type="italic">Kerî</hi> נפשׁי is old and acknowledged by the oldest authorities.<note placement="foot">The reading נפשׁי is adopted by Saadia (in <hi type="italic">Enumoth</hi> ii., where נפשׁי is equivalent to שׁמי), Juda ha-Levi (<hi type="italic">Cuzari</hi> iii. 27), Abulwalid (<hi type="italic">Rikma</hi> p. 180), Rashi, Kimchi, the Sohar, the Codices (and among others by that of the year 1294) and most editions (among which, the <hi type="italic">Complutensis</hi> has נפשׁי in the text). Nor does Aben-Ezra, whom Norzi has misunderstood, by any means reverse the relation of the <hi type="italic">Chethîb</hi> and <hi type="italic">Kerî</hi>; to him נפשׁי is the <hi type="italic">Kerî</hi>, and he explains it as a metaphor (an anthropomorphism): וכתוב נפשי דוך כנוי. Elias Levita is the only one who rejects the <hi type="italic">Kerî</hi> נפשׁי; but he does so though misunderstanding a Masora (vid., Baer’s <hi type="italic">Psalterium</hi> p. 130) and not without admitting Masoretic testimony in favour of it (וכן ראיתי ברוב נוסחאות המסורת). He is the only textual critic who rejects it. For Jacob b. Chajim is merely astonished that נפשׁו is not to be found in the Masoreth register of words written with <hi type="italic">Waw</hi> and to be read with <hi type="italic">Jod</hi>. And even Norzi does not reject this <hi type="italic">Kerî</hi>, which he is obliged to admit has greatly preponderating testimony in its favour, and he would only too gladly get rid of it.</note> <div eID="gen9296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9297" type="x-p"/> Even the lxx <hi type="italic">Cod. Alex</hi>. translates: τὴν ψυχὴν μου; whereas <hi type="italic">Cod. Vat.</hi> (Eus., Apollin., Theodor., et al.): τὴν ψυχὴν αὐτοῦ. Critically it is just as intangible, as it is exegetically incomprehensible; נפשׁי might then be equivalent to שׁמי. <reference osisRef="Exod.20.7">Exo 20:7</reference>, an explanation, however, which does not seem possible even from <reference osisRef="Amos.6.8">Amo 6:8</reference>; Jer 51:14. We let this <hi type="italic">Kerî</hi> alone to its undisturbed critical rights. But that the poet did actually write thus, is incredible. <div eID="gen9297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9298" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Ps.24.5">Psa 24:5</reference> (just as at the close of <reference osisRef="Ps.15.1-Ps.15.5">Psa 15:1-5</reference>), in continued predicates, we are told the character of the man, who is worthy of this privilege, to whom the question in <reference osisRef="Ps.24.3">Psa 24:3</reference> refers. Such an one shall bear away, or acquire (נשׁא, as e.g., <reference osisRef="Esth.2.17">Est 2:17</reference>) blessing from Jahve and righteousness from the God of his salvation (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.5">Psa 25:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.27.9">Psa 27:9</reference>). Righteousness, i.e., conformity to God and that which is well-pleasing to God, appears here as a gift, and in this sense it is used interchangeably with ישׁע (e.g., <reference osisRef="Ps.132.9">Psa 132:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.132.16">Psa 132:16</reference>). It is the righteousness of God after which the righteous, but not the self-righteous, man hungers and thirsts; that moral perfection which is the likeness of God restored to him and at the same time brought about by his own endeavours; it is the being changed, or transfigured, into the image of the Holy One Himself. With <reference osisRef="Ps.24.5">Psa 24:5</reference> the answer to the question of <reference osisRef="Ps.24.3">Psa 24:3</reference> is at an end; <reference osisRef="Ps.24.6">Psa 24:6</reference> adds that those thus qualified, who may accordingly expect to receive God’s gifts of salvation, are the true church of Jahve, the Israel of God. דּור (lit., a revolution, Arabic <hi type="italic">dahr</hi>, root דר, to turn, revolve) is used here, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.14.5">Psa 14:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.73.15">Psa 73:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.112.2">Psa 112:2</reference>, of a collective whole, whose bond of union is not contemporaneousness, but similarity of disposition; and it is an alliteration with the דּרשׁיו (<hi type="italic">Chethîb</hi> דרשו, without the <hi type="italic">Jod</hi> <hi type="italic">plur</hi>.) which follows. מבקשׁי פּניך is a second genitive depending on דּור, as in Psa 27:8. Here at the close the predication passes into the form of invocation (Thy face). And יעקב is a summarising predicate: in short, these are Jacob, not merely after the flesh, but after the spirit, and thus in truth (<reference osisRef="Isa.44.2">Isa 44:2</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Rom.9.6">Rom 9:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.6.16">Gal 6:16</reference>). By interpolating אלהי, as is done in the lxx and Peshîto, and adopted by Ewald, Olshausen, Hupfeld, and Böttcher, the nerve, as it were, of the assertion is cut through. The predicate, which has been expressed in different ways, is concentrated intelligibly enough in the one word יעקב, towards which it all along tends. And here the music becomes <hi type="italic">forte</hi>. The first part of this double Psalm dies away amidst the playing of the instruments of the Levitical priests; for the Ark was brought in בּכל־עז וּבשׁירים, as <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.5">2Sa 6:5</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.14">2Sa 6:14</reference>) is to be read.
entries.511009109f7febef3272faf4cb853e2361b963d8: <reference osisRef="Ps.24.7-Ps.24.10">Psa 24:7-10</reference> <div eID="gen9298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9299" type="x-p"/> The festal procession has now arrived above at the gates of the citadel of Zion. These are called פּתחי עולם, doors of eternity (not “of the world” as Luther renders it contrary to the Old Testament usage of the language) either as doors which pious faith hopes will last for ever, as Hupfeld and Hitzig explain it, understanding them, in opposition to the inscription of the Psalm, to be the gates of Solomon’s Temple; or, what seems to us much more appropriate in the mouth of those who are now standing before the gates, as the portals dating back into the hoary ages of the past (עולם as e.g., in <reference osisRef="Gen.49.26">Gen 49:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.58.12">Isa 58:12</reference>), the time of the Jebusites, and even of Melchizedek, though which the King of Glory, whose whole being and acts is glory, is now about to enter. It is the gates of the citadel of Zion, to which the cry is addressed, to expand themselves in a manner worthy of the Lord who is about to enter, for whom they are too low and too strait. Rejoicing at the great honour, thus conferred upon them, they are to raise their heads (<reference osisRef="Job.10.15">Job 10:15</reference>; Zec 2:4), i.e., lift up their portals (lintels); the doors of antiquity are to open high and wide.<note placement="foot">On the <hi type="italic">Munach</hi> instead of <hi type="italic">Metheg</hi> in והנּשׂיאוּ, vid., Baer’s <hi type="italic">Accentsystem</hi> vii. 2.</note> <div eID="gen9299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9300" type="x-p"/> Then the question echoes back to the festal procession from Zion’s gates which are wont only to admit mighty lords: who, then (זה giving vividness to the question, Ges. §122, 2), is this King of Glory; and they describe Him more minutely: it is the Hero-god, by whom Israel has wrested this Zion from the Jebusites with the sword, and by whom he has always been victorious in time past. The adjectival climactic form עזּוּז (like למּוּד, with <hi type="italic">ı̆</hi> instead of the <hi type="italic">ă</hi>in חנּוּן, קשּׁוּב) is only found in one other passage, viz., Isa 43:17. גּבּור מלחמה refers back to Exo 15:3. Thus then shall the gates raise their heads and the ancient doors lift themselves, i.e., open high and wide; and this is expressed here by <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> instead of <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>. (נשׂא to lift one’s self up, rise, as in <reference osisRef="Nah.1.5">Nah 1:5</reference>; Hos 13:1; <reference osisRef="Hab.1.3">Hab 1:3</reference>), according to the well-known order in which recurring verses and refrain-like repetitions move gently onwards. The gates of Zion ask once more, yet now no longer hesitatingly, but in order to hear more in praise of the great King. It is now the enquiry seeking fuller information; and the heaping up of the pronouns (as in <reference osisRef="Jer.30.21">Jer 30:21</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.46.7">Psa 46:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Esth.7.5">Est 7:5</reference>) expresses its urgency (<hi type="italic">quis tandem, ecquisnam</hi>). The answer runs, “Jahve Tsebaoth, He is the King of Glory (now making His entry).” צבאות ה is the proper name of Jahve as King, which had become His customary name in the time of the kings of Israel. צבאות is a genitive governed by ה and, while it is otherwise found only in reference to human hosts, in this combination it gains, of itself, the reference to the angels and the stars, which are called צבאיו in <reference osisRef="Ps.103.21">Psa 103:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.148.2">Psa 148:2</reference> : Jahve’s hosts consisting of celestial heroes, <reference osisRef="Joel.2.11">Joe 2:11</reference>, and of stars standing on the plain of the havens as it were in battle array, <reference osisRef="Isa.40.26">Isa 40:26</reference> -a reference for which experiences and utterances like those recorded in Gen 32:2., <reference osisRef="Deut.33.2">Deu 33:2</reference>; Jdg 5:20, have prepared the way. It is, therefore, the Ruler commanding innumerable and invincible super-terrestrial powers, who desires admission. The gates are silent and open wide; and Jahve, sitting enthroned above the Cherubim of the sacred Ark, enters into Zion.  <chapter eID="Ps.24"/> <div eID="gen9300" type="x-p"/>

entries.2175449d277826064e16a1e46008a73d14bb17af:
PSALM 24.
As God stands related to all mankind as their Creator and Governor, David, from this consideration, magnifies the special favor which God manifested towards the children of Abraham, in choosing them to be his peculiar people, in preference to the rest of mankind, and in erecting his sanctuary as his house that he might dwell among them. He shows, at the same time, that although the sanctuary was open to all the Jews, God was not near to all of them, but only to those who feared and served him in sincerity, and who had cleansed themselves from the pollutions of the world, in order to devote themselves to holiness and righteousness. Moreover, as the grace of God was more clearly manifested after the temple was built, he celebrates that grace in a strain of splendid poetry, to encourage true believers with the more alacrity to persevere in the exercise of serving and honoring him.
A Psalm of David.
Psalm 24:1-4
1. The earth is Jehovah’s, and the fullness thereof;
“Son contenu.” — Note, Fr. marg. “That is, its contents.”
the world, and they that dwell therein: 2. For he hath founded it upon the seas, and established it upon the floods. 3. Who shall ascend unto the hill of Jehovah? who shall stand in his holy place? 4. He who is clean of hands, and pure of heart; who hath not lifted up his soul to vanity, nor sworn deceitfully.
 
1. The earth is Jehovah’s. We will find in many other places the children of Abraham compared with all the rest of mankind, that the free goodness of God, in selecting them from all other nations, and in embracing them with his favor, may shine forth the more conspicuously. The object of the beginning of the psalm is to show that the Jews had nothing of themselves which could entitle them to approach nearer or more familiarly to God than the Gentiles. As God by his providence preserves the world, the power of his government is alike extended to all, so that he ought to be worshipped by all, even as he also shows to all men, without exception, the fatherly care he has about them. But since he preferred the Jews to all other nations, it was indispensably necessary that there should be some sacred bond of connection between him and them, which might distinguish them from the heathen nations. By this argument David invites and exhorts them to holiness. He tells them that it was reasonable that those whom God had adopted as his children, should bear certain marks peculiar to themselves, and not be altogether like strangers. Not that he incites them to endeavor to prejudice God against others, in order to gain his exclusive favor; but he teaches them, from the end or design of their election, that they shall then have secured to them the firm and peaceful possession of the honor which God had conferred upon them above other nations, when they devote themselves to an upright and holy life.
“Qu’adonc ils entrerent en ferme et paisible possession de l’honneur que Dieu leur a fait par dessus les autres nations.” — Fr.
In vain would they have been collected together into a distinct body, as the peculiar people of God, if they did not apply themselves to the cultivation of holiness. In short, the Psalmist pronounces God to be the King of the whole world, to let all men know that, even by the law of nature, they are bound to serve him. And by declaring that he made a covenant of salvation with a small portion of mankind, and by the erection of the tabernacle, gave the children of Abraham the symbol of his presence, thereby to assure them of his dwelling in the midst of them, he teaches them that they must endeavor to have purity of heart and of hands, if they would be accounted the members of his sacred family.
With respect to the word fullness, I admit that under it all the riches with which the earth is adorned are comprehended, as is proved by the authority of Paul; but I have no doubt that the Psalmist intends by the expression men themselves, who are the most illustrious ornament and glory of the earth. If they should fail, the earth would exhibit a scene of desolation and solitude, not less hideous than if God should despoil it of all its other riches. To what purpose are there produced so many kinds of fruit, and in so great abundance, and why are there so many pleasant and delightful countries, if it is not for the use and comfort of men?
“Car a quelle fin font produits des fruits de tant de sortes, et en telle abondance, et qu’il y a tant de vieux de plaisance, si non pour l’usage et commodite des hommes?” — Fr.
Accordingly, David explains, in the following clause, that it is principally of men that he speaks. It is his usual manner to repeat the same thing twice, and here the fullness of the earth, and the inhabitants of the world, have the same meaning. I do not, however, deny that the riches with which the earth abounds for the use of men, are comprehended under these expressions. Paul, therefore, (1 Corinthians 10:26) when discoursing concerning meats, justly quotes this passage in support of his argument, maintaining that no kind of food is unclean, because, “the earth is the Lord’s, and the fullness thereof.”

                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> Lift up your heads, O ye gates, and be ye lift up, ye<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> everlasting doors <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">So the Sence is, that seek the true Church, here called <ns0:hi>Iacob,</ns0:hi> that desire the knowledge of it, and Conversation with it, in which Sence many are said to <ns0:hi>seek Solomons Face,</ns0:hi> as the Phrase is in the Hebrew, 1 <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> 10. 24. 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 9. 23. and the Harlot to <ns0:hi>seek</ns0:hi> her Lovers <ns0:hi>Face<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Prov.</ns0:hi> 7. 15. And so this is by some expounded of the <ns0:hi>Gentiles,</ns0:hi> who enquired after the true Church, and finding it in <ns0:hi>Iacob,</ns0:hi> were desirous to become Proselytes, and to joyn themselves to the Church of <ns0:hi>Iacob</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Israel.</ns0:hi> But it must be remembred that the Psalmist is not here speaking, of the calling of the <ns0:hi>Gentiles,</ns0:hi> but only of the Cha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />racter or Qualification of the true <ns0:hi>Iacobites</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Israelites,</ns0:hi> who cannot conveniently be said to <ns0:hi>seek the Face of Iacob, (i. e.)</ns0:hi> Their own. And the Phrase of <ns0:hi>seeking the Face of Iacob</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>of the Church,</ns0:hi> is no where used in Scripture. Or, as it is in the Margent, <ns0:hi>O God of Iacob.</ns0:hi> But that seems to be too large a Supplement<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Or<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> this is <ns0:hi>Iacob,</ns0:hi> the Pronoun <ns0:hi>this</ns0:hi> being ea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sily understood out of the beginning of the Verse. Or, the Generation (which may in the same manner be supplied) of <ns0:hi>Iacob, Iacob</ns0:hi> being here put not for the Person, but for the posterity, of <ns0:hi>Iacob,</ns0:hi> as it is <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 49. 7. <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 23. 7. 10. 23. <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 32. 9. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 14. 7. or for the Church or people of God, which is oft called <ns0:hi>Iacob</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 14. 1. and 41. 8. and 44. 1, 5, 21. &c. So the Sence is, this and this only is the true <ns0:hi>Iacob</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> or Church of God, and all others are so only in Name and Title, although they be descended lineally from him. Or, in <ns0:hi>Iacob,</ns0:hi> the Particle <ns0:hi>in</ns0:hi> being here under<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stood, as it is in <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 2. 12. and 17. 12. and in many other places. So the Sence of the place is, this is the true Genera<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion of them, that seek God's Face in <ns0:hi>Iacob. (i. e.</ns0:hi>) Either in <ns0:hi>Iacobs</ns0:hi> Land, or Sanctuary, the only place where God was to be sought: Or, among the <ns0:hi>Iacobites,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Israelites.</ns0:hi> By which he insinuates, what is expressed, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 9. 6. that, <ns0:hi>all are not Israel, that are of Israel,</ns0:hi> and that all were not <ns0:hi>Israelites</ns0:hi> in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />deed, that were sprung from <ns0:hi>Iacob,</ns0:hi> but only those of them who were such as he described, v. 4. Comp. <ns0:hi>Io<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>.</ns0:hi> 1. 47. <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 228, 29.</ns0:note> and the King of glory <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">The question was put; Who shall ascend into God's Hill and Holy place, v. 3. To which Answer hath been given, and the Persons described, v. 4, 5, 6. But because there still were impediments in the way, and there were <ns0:hi>Gates</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Doors</ns0:hi> to this Holy place, to shut out those who would ascend thither, therefore he poetically speaks to those <ns0:hi>Gates,</ns0:hi> to o<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pen and let in the King of Glory, who would make way for his Subjects and followers. Here is a Representation of a Triumphant entrance of a King into his Royal City and Pa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lace; for which the Gates use to be enlarged, or at least Wide opened. He speaks here of the <ns0:hi>Gates</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Doors,</ns0:hi> Either, 1<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Of his Royal City of <ns0:hi>Sion,</ns0:hi> through which the Ark was at this time to be brought to the Tabernacle, which <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> had built for it, called <ns0:hi>Everlasting,</ns0:hi> Either from the solidity and durableness of the Matter, or from <ns0:hi>David's</ns0:hi> Desires and Hopes, that God would make them such in some sort, because he <ns0:hi>loved the Gates of Sion, Psal.</ns0:hi> 87. 2<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Or rather, 2. Of the Temple, which by Faith and the Spirit of Prophecy, he be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />held as already built, and accordingly addresseth his Speech to it, whose <ns0:hi>Doors</ns0:hi> he calls <ns0:hi>Everlasting,</ns0:hi> not so much because they were made of strong and durable Materials, as in Op<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />position of those of the Tabernacle, which were removed from place to place, whereas the Temple and it's Doors were constantly fixed in one place, and, if the sins of <ns0:hi>Israel</ns0:hi> did not hinder <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>were to abide there for ever, (<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) As long as the Mosaical dispensation was to last, or until the coming of the Messias, as that Phrase is very commonly taken in the Old Testament. These Gates he bids <ns0:hi>li<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>t up their Heads,</ns0:hi> or Tops either by allusion, to those Gates which have a Portcullis at the top of them, which may be let down or taken up, and ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cordingly makes the Entrance either higher and lower: Or, that by this figurative Address to the Gates, he might signi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fie the Duty of the People, to make their Gates higher and Wider, to give their King a more Magnificent entrance. But though this be the litteral Sence of the place, yet there is al<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />so a Mystical Sence of it, and that too designed by the Holy Ghost. And as the Temple was undoubtedly a Type of Christ, and of his Church, and of Heaven it self, so this place may also contain a Representation, Either of Christ<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> s entrance into his Church, or into the Hearts of his faithful People, who are here Commanded to set open their Hearts and Souls, which are not unfitly called <ns0:hi>everlasting Doors,</ns0:hi> for his Reception: Or of his Ascension into Heaven, where the Saints or Angels are poetically introduced as preparing the way, and opening the Heavenly Gates to receive their Lord and King, returning to his Royal Habitation, with Triumph and Glory. Comp. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 47. 5. and 68. 25. <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 2. 33. <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 4. 8.</ns0:note> shall come in. <ns0:note place="bottom">

                           </ns0:gap>ovah,</ns0:hi> who dwelt in the Temple, and between the Cherubims, Or the Messias, the King of <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> and of his Church, called <ns0:hi>the King,</ns0:hi> Or <ns0:hi>Lord of Glory,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 2. 8. <ns0:hi>Iam.</ns0:hi>

                  <ns0:p n="8">8. Who <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> the King of glory <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">This seems to be a Prolepsis, or removal of an Objection: You will say, What is the cause of this imperi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ous Call? and why, or for whom must those Gates be open<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed, in so solemn and Extraordinary a manner?</ns0:note>? the LORD strong and mighty, the LORD mighty in bat<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tel <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">This contains an Answer to the question, He is no ordi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nary Person, no meaner and no other than <ns0:hi>Iehovah,</ns0:hi> who hath given so many Proofs of his Almightiness, who hath sub<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dued all his Enemies, and is now returned in Triumph. Here is in this, and the foregoing Verse, a sacred Dialogue between several Persons. And some suppose that the Sacred Musitians, which attended upon the Service of the Ark and Tabernacle, and were doubtless employed in this Solemnity, 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 6. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>. were divided into two Quires, whereof one spake the former, and the other the latter Verse.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

Lift up your heads, O ye gates, even lift <ns0:hi>them</ns0:hi> up, ye everlasting doors, and the King of glory shall come in <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">The same Verse is repeated again, Partly to shame and a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />waken the Dulness of mankind, who are so hardly brought to a serious Preparation for such Solemnities: and Partly, to sig<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nifie the great worth and importance of the Matter, contain<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed under these Expressions.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10. Who is <ns0:hi>this</ns0:hi> King of glory? the LORD of host <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Under whose Command are all the Hosts of Heaven and Earth, Angels and Men, and all other Creatures.</ns0:note>, he <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> the King of glory, Selah.</ns0:p>
